segments.title: The treaty category that small carriers never received
segments.body: The 1930 negotiations missed an opportunity to distinguish fleet carriers from smaller light or escort carriers. Larger ships were already understood to be more efficient for fleet aviation, yet fears that Japan might mass-produce small carriers shaped the rules. Henderson had only just taken charge of the Royal Navy's carrier organization, while the solutions he would develop by 1933 still lay ahead. British experience with aviation in First World War anti-submarine operations and prewar studies of merchant conversions show that convoy carriers were under consideration long before war began. The missed category narrowed the options available for both fleet aviation and convoy protection before the wartime emergency.

evidence.note: Fear that Japan would mass-produce small carriers discouraged a separate small-carrier category even though Britain had already considered convoy carriers and merchant conversions.

segments.summary: Fear of Japanese small-carrier construction discouraged a category that could have supported convoy protection and anti-submarine aviation.

segments.title: Treaty rules and wartime contingency planning
segments.body: Britain may have supported American efforts to restrict Japanese carrier construction while planning to apply other treaty clauses pragmatically. A foreign warship still in a British yard provides the hypothetical example: if war began before delivery, Britain might have retained it. This is a speculative contingency rather than a claim that seizure was certain. Peacetime arms-control commitments could coexist with emergency fleet-acquisition planning.

evidence.note: British support for carrier limits compared with a hypothetical wartime takeover of a foreign warship still in a British yard.

segments.summary: British support for restricting Japanese construction could coexist with plans to interpret acquisition rules pragmatically if war intervened.

segments.title: A two-tier fleet and light-carrier system
segments.body: Several possible formulas reserve most tonnage for fleet carriers while protecting a smaller allocation for light carriers. An 8,188-long-ton reference point shows how far a useful aviation hull could sit below fleet-carrier size. Permission to build sub-10,000-ton light carriers might even have removed the perceived need for HMS Unicorn in its historical form. USS Wasp's 14,700-long-ton standard displacement later provides a concrete example of what a 15,000-ton ceiling could accommodate. The arithmetic is awkward, but the purpose is clear: prevent every navy from spending its entire allowance on one carrier type. For the Royal Navy, such a rule could have supported a repeating program of roughly 25,000-ton fleet carriers and 11,000- to 15,000-ton light carriers without a carrier-building holiday.

evidence.note: Fleet-carrier and light-carrier tonnage divisions and likely British construction choices.
USS Wasp displaced 14,700 long tons standard, demonstrating what a 15,000-ton carrier category could produce.

segments.summary: A proposed division of carrier tonnage between fleet and light ships explores how treaty rules could encourage a more varied aviation fleet.

segments.title: Why the 1936 rules quickly lost practical force
segments.body: This counterfactual folds the 1936 rules into the 1930 settlement instead of treating the later treaty as a durable independent regime. The later agreement constrained its signatories without securing the participation of several powers they considered possible opponents. That asymmetry made the system increasingly theoretical by 1937. Treasuries could still invoke treaty limits because they reduced expenditure, but military planners could not treat them as dependable common restraints. Britain's formal Ten Year Rule had already ended in 1932, showing the widening gap between economy measures and security assumptions.

evidence.note: The 1936 treaty lacked participation from several potential opponents, but Treasury pressure to preserve its savings continued after the Ten Year Rule ended in 1932.

segments.summary: Major potential opponents remained outside the later agreement, leaving treasuries to invoke its savings after its strategic bargain had weakened.

segments.title: What Glorious and Courageous still offered
segments.body: Glorious and Courageous were imperfect conversions, but neither was militarily irrelevant. Each could carry about 48 aircraft by 1939, giving the ships meaningful operational weight. A fuller modernization could have extended their flight decks, hangars, lifts, and aircraft capacity. Had they survived, extra carriers at Mers-el-Kebir, during the Bismarck hunt, or at other crisis points could have added striking power while reducing wear on the rest of the fleet.

evidence.note: The transcript assesses modernization possibilities and wartime uses for Glorious and Courageous.

segments.summary: The converted battlecruisers remained useful 48-aircraft carriers whose survival could have eased pressure on Britain's wartime carrier force.

segments.title: Carrier building as Depression-era economic policy
segments.body: The scenario keeps the 1929 Wall Street Crash because removing it would sever too many links with actual interwar history. Governments instead adopt a more active Keynesian approach and treat naval orders as one form of economic intervention. Stanley Baldwin replaces Ramsay MacDonald and Al Smith replaces Herbert Hoover because the counterfactual assumes they would be more willing to fund defence and employment. Those political changes supply the demand needed to keep carrier construction, design work, and skilled maritime labour moving through the Depression.

evidence.note: The transcript preserves the Wall Street Crash while using Keynesian policy, Baldwin, and Smith to justify greater naval construction.

segments.summary: The counterfactual keeps the Wall Street Crash but changes political choices so naval construction can support skilled industry and national recovery.

segments.title: How naval treaties are negotiated outside the formal room
segments.body: The conference chamber presents hierarchy and public positions, but much of the agreement is prepared in quieter discussions around it. The seating plan still displays authority, with senior delegates at the table and aides arranged behind them by rank. Delegates normally test allied support before speaking formally and frame proposals to constrain or surprise opponents. This makes arms control a contest of coalition management and wording as much as ship numbers.

evidence.note: The relationship between formal sessions, sidebars, allied support, and tactical wording.

segments.summary: Formal speeches display agreed positions, while side conversations do much of the real work of assembling a treaty coalition.

segments.title: Article I paused capital ships, not all warships
segments.body: Article I halted the laying down of replacement capital ships from 1931 through 1936. This covered battleships and battlecruisers or fast battleships, rather than every category of naval construction. Aircraft carriers were outside this particular holiday. Describing the treaty as a general ban on shipbuilding therefore misreads its scope.

evidence.note: Article I suspended the laying down of replacement capital ships from 1931 through 1936; it did not ban all naval construction or include aircraft carriers.

segments.summary: The 1931-1936 replacement holiday applied to capital ships rather than imposing a general ban on naval construction.

segments.title: The 1930 treaty defines the aircraft carrier
segments.body: The treaty replaces the Washington definition with one centered on a warship's exclusive purpose and its ability to launch and land aircraft. Merely fitting a flying-off platform to another ship type did not make it a carrier. A further prohibition on landing decks for existing capital ships reflects anxiety that navies might combine battleship and carrier capabilities in one hull. These definitions prevented a navy from escaping carrier rules simply by presenting aviation equipment as an accessory to another combatant.

evidence.note: Article 3 defines a carrier by the exclusive purpose of launching and landing aircraft and bars landing decks on existing capital ships, preventing hybrid battlecarriers.

segments.summary: Article 3 classifies purpose-built flight-deck ships as carriers while preventing existing capital ships from becoming hybrid battlecarriers.

segments.title: Why the 10,000-ton rule chilled small-carrier construction
segments.body: Article 4 focuses on carriers of 10,000 tons or less carrying guns above 6.1 inches, then repeats restrictions on acquisition and construction. The repetition made small-carrier projects appear politically risky even where a narrow legal reading might permit them. Under the Washington Treaty, carriers below 10,000 tons had sat outside the national carrier allowance. The London rules brought them into the tonnage accounting, so a small carrier now consumed scarce allowance even if its construction remained technically possible. Article 5 standardized the carrier gun ceiling at 6.1 inches.

evidence.note: Articles 4 and 5 counted small carriers toward national tonnage, repeated restrictions on their acquisition and construction, and capped their guns at 6.1 inches, discouraging the category.
The later recap contrasts the Washington exclusion for sub-10,000-ton carriers with their inclusion in London Treaty tonnage.

segments.summary: Repeated restrictions around small carriers and guns created enough ambiguity to deter navies and their treasuries from using the category.

segments.title: First World War trauma shaped the treaty mindset
segments.body: King George V belonged to a governing class scarred by the loss of friends, relatives, and a generation of junior leaders. The especially high exposure of junior officers and junior NCOs made wartime death immediate within political and social networks. That experience encouraged peace-seeking and caution in Britain and France. Germany's evolving stab-in-the-back myth shows how another defeated society could interpret the war differently. Japan had fought a comparatively successful and less costly war, so its leaders did not necessarily share Anglo-French assumptions. Treaty makers risked mistaking their own trauma for a universal strategic outlook.

evidence.note: George V and elite wartime losses in relation to peace policy, compared with Japanese experience and expectations.

segments.summary: British and French leaders negotiated from deep wartime loss, while Japan's different experience produced a sharply different view of risk and victory.

segments.title: The 1936 treaty narrows carrier size and armament
segments.body: The 1936 rules lower maximum standard displacement to 23,000 tons and retain the 6.1-inch gun ceiling, with no more than ten guns above 5.25 inches. They also distinguish conventional flight-deck carriers from ships without such a deck, leaving seaplane carriers inside the framework. A twenty-year service rule permits old carriers to be replaced rather than freezing the category indefinitely. Ark Royal shows how much capability could still fit within roughly 22,000 long tons.

evidence.note: The 1936 treaty capped carriers at 23,000 tons and 6.1-inch guns, limited guns above 5.25 inches to ten, distinguished flight-deck and seaplane-carrier categories, and permitted replacement after twenty years.

segments.summary: The later treaty sets a 23,000-ton limit, caps heavy guns, defines flight-deck and non-flight-deck carrier categories, and permits replacement after twenty years.

segments.title: A treaty needs ships Japan can actually build
segments.body: The proposed 10:10:7:4:4 ratio would give Japan a visible gain while preserving Anglo-American superiority. A Japanese construction program would consume money, labour, and industrial capacity that could not simultaneously support every other military ambition. Permitting useful ships within the agreement could make continued membership more attractive than a dramatic breakout. Construction would then operate as a concession and a restraint, buying time by giving Japan something valuable to lose.

evidence.note: Building to the proposed 10:10:7:4:4 ratio would consume Japanese resources while giving Japan a reason to remain under treaty limits rather than pursue an unrestricted breakout.

segments.summary: A workable ratio could absorb Japanese resources, buy time, and reduce the incentive to abandon treaty limits for much larger carriers.

segments.title: British carrier numbers versus American carrier size
segments.body: The Washington framework nominally allowed 27,000-ton carriers and larger 33,000-ton conversions. Courageous and Glorious displaced only about 24,210 long tons, even though Britain could have used more of the conversion allowance. That choice fits the Royal Navy's preference for enough viable carriers to cover widely separated commitments. Lexington and Saratoga show the American alternative, concentrating far more tonnage and aviation capacity in each hull.

evidence.note: The transcript reviews Washington carrier limits, British conversion displacement, and the Royal Navy preference for numbers over maximum size.

segments.summary: Washington Treaty allowances encouraged the Royal Navy to spread aviation across more hulls while the United States concentrated capability in much larger conversions.

segments.title: Strike carriers and fleet carriers answered different missions
segments.body: Illustrious and Ark Royal embody different answers to how the Royal Navy expected carriers to fight. Armour on Illustrious reduced the number of aircraft she could carry for her roughly 23,000-long-ton displacement. Strike carriers were designed around the air group for attacks such as Taranto, while fleet carriers remained with the moving fleet to scout, provide fighter defence, and deliver strikes. The strike carrier served as concentrated offensive power at the admiral's direction. Air-group size therefore has to be judged alongside a carrier's assigned mission and protection scheme.

evidence.note: Illustrious's armour reduced her air group, whereas an Ark Royal-style strike carrier concentrated aircraft for missions such as Taranto.

segments.summary: Ark Royal and Illustrious illustrate how air-group size, armour, and assigned mission pulled British carrier designs in different directions.

segments.title: Why geography pushed Britain toward armoured carriers
segments.body: Britain expected its carriers to operate either far from home infrastructure in the Far East or under unavoidable land-based air threat in the Mediterranean. In the Far East, damage control and repairability mattered because ships would be remote from the home industrial base. Metal structures were easier to repair and store in a humid overseas environment than wood. In the Mediterranean, Italian airfields made attack difficult to avoid. The Royal Navy's interwar threat hierarchy placed Japan first, Italy second, and rearming Germany as an emerging third concern. Because Italy sat across the route to the Far East, carrier survival in the Mediterranean was directly connected to reinforcing the theatre where Britain expected its largest naval threat.

evidence.note: Britain needed carriers that could be repaired far from home in the Far East and survive land-based air attack in the Mediterranean; its interwar threat order placed Japan first, Italy second, and Germany third.

segments.summary: British carrier design emphasized survival and repair because likely wars placed ships far from yards or within range of land-based aircraft.

segments.title: Lexington and Saratoga set the real carrier benchmark
segments.body: Although often paired with Courageous and Glorious, USS Lexington and USS Saratoga were substantially larger ships. Their nominal 33,000-ton treaty figure gained another 3,000 tons through allowances for torpedo defence and other protection. An equitable system could acknowledge that real benchmark and then divide a larger total allowance between fleet and light carriers. Using actual displacement rather than the paper limit would prevent the American conversions from becoming an unspoken advantage inside a supposedly common system.

evidence.note: Lexington and Saratoga reached about 36,000 long tons after a 3,000-ton protection allowance, well above the British conversions used in comparison.

segments.summary: The American conversions reached about 36,000 long tons, making them a more honest basis for equitable limits than smaller British conversions.

segments.title: A steady carrier program instead of a wartime rush
segments.body: The counterfactual does not assume Britain instantly builds to its full treaty allowance. Instead, one fleet carrier and one light carrier enter production on alternating years, establishing a sustainable replacement rhythm. The example uses two-year building cycles rather than ships completed in a single budget year. It sketches fleet-carrier completions in 1932, 1934, 1936, and 1938, with light carriers arriving in the intervening years. By 1939 this could yield several modern ships while keeping design teams, yards, and skilled labor active for emergency expansion.

evidence.note: Alternating fleet- and light-carrier orders and plausible commissioning years.

segments.summary: Alternating fleet and light-carrier orders could preserve yards and deliver a balanced force gradually across a twenty-year replacement cycle.

segments.title: Ryūjō embodied the fear behind the small-carrier rules
segments.body: The 1930 provisions brought sub-10,000-ton carriers into treaty tonnage and constrained their armament, making large programs less attractive. That change removed the Washington-era advantage of building small carriers outside the national allowance. Ryūjō illustrates both why other powers worried and why the concept had limits. Japan tried to obtain substantial aviation utility from a very small displacement, but the resulting ship suffered serious topweight and operating problems.

evidence.note: The treaty made sub-10,000-ton carriers consume national tonnage; Ryūjō showed that such a hull could be useful but suffered serious topweight and stability costs.

segments.summary: Japan's attempt to combine fleet and escort-carrier value in a roughly 10,000-ton hull produced a useful but chronically top-heavy ship.

segments.title: The proposed equitable carrier settlement
segments.body: The alternative starts from a ratio Japan might regard as a diplomatic victory while Britain and the United States retain meaningful superiority. Anglo-American intelligence had identified that ratio as something Japanese negotiators valued, opening room for concessions elsewhere in exchange. Existing Lexington-class ships would be acknowledged, but future builds would be capped around 31,000 tons with 6.1-inch guns and a twenty-year replacement life. A ten-carrier, 310,000-ton ceiling offers flexibility in ship size without encouraging unlimited mass construction. An acceptable headline ratio could keep Japan invested in the wider agreement.

evidence.note: The proposed ratio, new-build limit, gun limit, replacement rule, ship count, and total tonnage.

segments.summary: A 10:10:7:4:4 ratio, a 31,000-ton new-build ceiling, and 310,000 total tons aim to give Japan security without surrendering Anglo-American superiority.

segments.title: How more tonnage changes British and American carriers
segments.body: Britain's historical division between an air-group-centred strike carrier and an armoured fleet carrier reflected tight design tradeoffs. In this counterfactual, extra displacement lets one design combine roles that the Royal Navy had divided between separate carrier types. Ships around 25,800 tons might pair Ark Royal's aviation capacity with more of Illustrious's protection. The United States could use a 31,000-ton ceiling for larger revised Yorktowns and avoid the compromised Wasp. Because American planning centred on a Pacific war, the same treaty space could sensibly produce larger air groups rather than an identical British-style design.

evidence.note: A larger allowance could merge Britain's strike and fleet-carrier roles in a roughly 25,800-ton design and let the United States build 31,000-ton Yorktown successors with larger air groups and better protection.

segments.summary: Extra displacement could merge Britain's strike and fleet roles while giving American Yorktown successors larger air groups and better protection.

segments.title: Carrier construction strengthens industry and deterrence
segments.body: Peacetime construction sustains the industrial capacity needed to rearm quickly while adding hulls to the fleet. Regular orders keep yards, skilled labour, and design experience available when emergency expansion begins. A visibly stronger British carrier force could also raise Germany's estimate of the force required for a successful war. Construction can therefore contribute to deterrence before the added ships ever fight.

evidence.note: Continuous carrier construction would speed wartime mobilization and require Germany to account for a larger British carrier force, potentially raising the threshold for a successful challenge.

segments.summary: A continuing building program creates both a stronger wartime production base and a larger force that adversaries must account for before choosing war.

segments.title: Why militaries cannot bet the state on unproven technology
segments.body: Promising technologies often accumulate confident theories before they are tested in war. Small civilian UAVs in Ukraine provide the 2022 example: they were supplying troops with information in ways some analysts had predicted, while other expectations remained uncertain. A disappointing result might reflect immature technology, the particulars of the conflict, or a faulty theory. Military planners therefore need a conservative margin when incorporating novel systems. Armed forces may be wagering national survival and lives when an untried concept fails.

evidence.note: UAV reporting from Ukraine illustrates technological uncertainty and the exceptional cost of failed military bets.

segments.summary: The 2022 UAV example shows why promising theories still require a conservative margin when failure could cost lives or national survival.

segments.title: Higher treaty limits favor the strongest shipbuilding powers
segments.body: USS Enterprise's 19,800-long-ton standard displacement shows that an effective carrier could sit well below the proposed maximum. More tonnage need not mean only larger ships; navies could choose more 20,000- to 22,000-ton carriers instead. A larger allowance did not guarantee that Congress or Parliament would fund every possible hull. It could also buy protection, as later American interest in the armoured Midway class suggests. Because Britain and the United States possessed the largest maritime industrial bases, they were better positioned to reach a higher ceiling than Japan. Japan would have to sacrifice other construction and spend years pursuing its allotted ratio, so nominal equality of access would still favor the powers best able to use it.

evidence.note: Alternative ship sizes, added protection, and the unequal industrial ability to use larger treaty allowances.

segments.summary: Britain and America could exploit larger allowances faster than Japan because their maritime industries and economies already had greater depth.

segments.title: Using limited fleets to bind Germany and the Soviet Union
segments.body: The proposed settlement could invite Germany and the Soviet Union into lower tiers rather than leave them outside the system. Soviet construction divided among the Baltic, Black Sea, Northern, and Pacific fleets would struggle to concentrate, but even a Far Eastern force would complicate Japanese planning. The 1939 Soviet-Japanese fighting shows how Far Eastern commitments could shape Soviet choices in Europe. A legal naval programme could also give the Weimar Republic a visible diplomatic success and maritime prestige that extremists might otherwise exploit. France would still retain twice Germany's allocation, while Britain would possess a much larger margin over Italy.

evidence.note: The transcript explores German and Soviet treaty tiers, Soviet fleet distribution, Japanese distraction, and Weimar political prestige.

segments.summary: Small treaty allocations might strengthen Weimar legitimacy while Soviet fleet construction divides attention between Germany and Japan.

segments.title: Why two carriers do not create a continuous capability
segments.body: A simple readiness ladder distinguishes possession from operational capability. One carrier is largely a prestige asset, while two normally allow only one ship to be available at a time. Three improve the odds of coverage, but four are needed to support a deployed ship, an immediate relief, and vessels passing through refit, training, transit, or dry-docking. Germany's proposed two-carrier allowance would create experience and options without guaranteeing continuous carrier operations.

evidence.note: One carrier offers prestige, two usually yield one available hull, three improve coverage, and four can sustain a deployment and relief while the remaining ships rotate through training, refit, transit, or dry-docking.

segments.summary: Carrier numbers must cover deployment, relief, training, refit, and dry-docking before a navy can guarantee that a ship is available.

segments.title: Multilateral limits instead of a later bilateral deal
segments.body: A small German allocation inside a multilateral agreement would provide a limit that all the signatories could monitor. It might remove the perceived need for the later Anglo-German Naval Agreement, which created friction with France. Soviet participation could similarly create a legal fleet while diverting Japanese attention in the Far East. An equitable settlement could pursue hard-nosed balance-of-power aims without repeating the humiliating, short-term victories that made later cooperation less likely.

evidence.note: A multilateral German limit could avoid the later Anglo-German Naval Agreement and its friction with France, while a crushing treaty victory would make future cooperation less likely.

segments.summary: Bringing Germany into the common treaty could impose limits without the diplomatic damage caused by the later Anglo-German Naval Agreement.

segments.title: Treaty tonnage, not indifference, constrained British carriers
segments.body: The alternative allowance would not automatically produce every permitted ship, and older carriers might still need to be retired to remain under the 310,000-ton ceiling. HMS Furious might have remained in service longer, though the enlarged allowance would not preserve every existing hull. Britain had six carriers in 1930 and soon seven, evidence of an existing institutional commitment to naval aviation. Implacable's later displacement shows how an extra few thousand tons could materially improve a British fleet carrier without demanding a radically larger design. The counterfactual changes design room and replacement pace while retaining financial and construction limits.

evidence.note: Treaty permission did not guarantee construction: Britain had six carriers in 1930 and soon seven under a 135,000-ton limit, while Implacable showed what extra displacement could add.

segments.summary: Britain already possessed the world's largest carrier count in 1930, but its 135,000-ton ceiling sharply limited replacement choices.
